config.title: Write pick generic with keyof

intro.title: Write pick generic with keyof
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom utility function called `myPick` that selects specific properties from an object. You'll learn how to use TypeScript's `keyof` operator to create a type-safe generic function that works with any object type. The main concepts involve generics, type constraints, and indexed access types to ensure the function returns only the requested keys. This exercise will help you understand how to write reusable, type-safe utilities in TypeScript.
intro.usecase: The `Pick` utility type is essential for creating type-safe, reusable components in large-scale applications. For example, when building a user profile dashboard, you might have a full `User` interface but only need to display a subset of fields like `name` and `email` in a summary panel. Using `Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>` ensures your component only accepts the required properties, preventing bugs and improving maintainability. This pattern is also common in form libraries, API response filtering, and configuration objects where you need to select specific properties from a larger type.

objectives: Implement a generic Pick type using keyof and mapped types
Apply the Pick generic to extract specific properties from existing interfaces
Construct type-safe functions that accept only selected object properties
Configure generic constraints to ensure keys exist on the source type
Manipulate object types by selecting subsets of their properties
Initialize variables with types derived from Pick generic usage
Integrate the Pick generic into existing type definitions and function signatures

steps.title: Create a basic TypeScript interface for a user object
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named 'User' with properties: id (number), name (string), email (string), and age (number).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface with four typed properties will be created.
successCriteria: The code contains an interface named User with id: number, name: string, email: string, and age: number properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that all four properties (id, name, email, age) are present with the correct TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword and define all four properties with their types.

steps.instruction: Create a constant named 'user' that is an object matching the User interface you defined in step 1.
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword followed by the object with properties that match the User interface types.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a typed user object that TypeScript can validate against the User interface.
successCriteria: A constant named 'user' is created with properties name (string), age (number), and email (string) that match the User interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your user object has all three properties (name, age, email) with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The user object doesn't match the User interface. Check that you have all required properties with the correct TypeScript types.

steps.title: Write a manual pick function without generics
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'manualPick' that takes a User object and an array of keys, and returns a new object with only those keys.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts two parameters: the object and an array of property names. Use a loop or reduce to build the result object.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that can extract specific properties from a User object.
successCriteria: The manualPick function is defined, takes a User object and keys array, and returns an object with only the specified keys.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function accepts both parameters and returns an object with only the specified keys.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't correctly pick properties. Check that it takes a User object and keys array, and returns an object with only those keys.

steps.title: Introduce the Pick generic type concept
steps.instruction: Create a new type named UserNameOnly that uses TypeScript's built-in Pick utility type to select only the 'name' property from the User interface.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: type NewType = Pick<ExistingType, 'propertyName'>. This creates a new type with just the selected property.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a new type UserNameOnly that represents an object with only the 'name' property from User, demonstrating how Pick works.
successCriteria: A UserNameOnly type is created using Pick<User, 'name'> syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct syntax: type UserNameOnly = Pick<User, 'name'>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UserNameOnly type wasn't created correctly. Remember to use Pick<User, 'name'> to select just the name property.

steps.title: Create a generic pick function signature
steps.instruction: Create a function signature for a generic pick function named 'genericPick' that takes two parameters: an object of type T and a key of type K, where K extends keyof T. Use a generic type parameter T and a constrained generic type parameter K.
steps.hint: Start with 'function genericPick<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { }' or use an arrow function with the same signature.
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic function signature that can pick properties from any object type using a key parameter.
successCriteria: The genericPick function is defined with generic type parameters T and K where K extends keyof T, and returns the type T[K].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function has both generic type parameters (T and K) and that K is constrained with 'extends keyof T'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature is missing required generic type parameters or constraints. Review the generic function syntax.

steps.title: Add keyof constraint to the generic type
steps.instruction: In your genericPick function signature, add a constraint to the K type parameter using keyof T to ensure K must be a valid key of T.
steps.hint: Use extends keyof T after the K type parameter in the function signature.
steps.expectedOutcome: The genericPick function signature now has a type constraint ensuring K must be a valid key of T.
successCriteria: The genericPick function signature includes K extends keyof T in its type parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the constraint isn't quite complete. Make sure K extends keyof T appears in the type parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The keyof constraint is missing. Remember to add K extends keyof T to restrict K to valid keys of T.

steps.title: Implement the pick function body
steps.instruction: Inside the genericPick function, implement the body to create and return a new object containing only the properties specified in the keys array.
steps.hint: You can use reduce or a for loop to iterate through the keys array and build the result object. Remember to return the result object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The genericPick function should have a working implementation that returns an object with only the specified keys.
successCriteria: The genericPick function body is implemented and returns a new object containing only the properties from the input object that match the keys array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started implementing the function body, but it's not complete. Make sure you're iterating through the keys array and building a result object to return.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function body implementation is missing or incorrect. Try using a loop or reduce to build a new object with only the specified properties from the input object.

steps.title: Add proper return type annotation
steps.instruction: Add a return type annotation to the genericPick function signature using the Pick utility type: Pick<T, K>.
steps.hint: After the parameter list, add a colon followed by Pick<T, K> to specify the function's return type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The genericPick function signature now includes a return type annotation using Pick<T, K>.
successCriteria: The genericPick function has a return type annotation of Pick<T, K>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added ': Pick<T, K>' after the parameter list in the function signature.
steps.feedbackWrong: The return type annotation is missing or incorrect. Add ': Pick<T, K>' after the parameter list.

steps.title: Compare manual and generic pick implementations
steps.instruction: Add a console.log statement that demonstrates the type safety difference between manualPick and genericPick by trying to access a non-existent property on each result.
steps.hint: Call both functions with the same user object and keys, then try to access a property that wasn't picked (like 'age') on each result. Log both attempts to see which one TypeScript catches as an error.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see that TypeScript correctly flags an error when trying to access 'age' on genericResult, but allows it on manualResult, demonstrating the type safety benefit of the generic pick function.
successCriteria: The console.log statement demonstrates that genericPick provides type safety by catching property access errors at compile time, while manualPick does not.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
